analysis_window.caution: 2015 is a partial year: the window starts 2015-06-30, so it holds roughly half a year of headlines. Raw counts are not comparable across years.

ifnd.name: IFND - Indian Fake News Dataset
ifnd.citation: Sharma, D. K., & Garg, S. (2021). IFND: a benchmark dataset for fake news detection. Complex & Intelligent Systems, 9, 2843-2863. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40747-021-00552-1
ifnd.license: See publisher terms; redistributed by the dataset authors on GitHub
ifnd.provenance: Author's own copy, github.com/sonalgarg174/Dataset. The Fake class is partly produced by an LSTM-based augmentation algorithm (real news 37,809 vs real fake 7,271 before augmentation), so reported accuracy is an upper bound and this limitation is stated in the report.

nifty.name: Nifty 50 daily index prices
nifty.citation: Mirror of Yahoo Finance daily OHLCV for ^NSEI, redistributed in github.com/manishkr1754/NIFTY50_Data_Analysis_NSETOOLS_NSEPY_Python
nifty.license: Unofficial redistribution of Yahoo Finance data
nifty.provenance: Unofficial GitHub mirror of Yahoo Finance ^NSEI daily OHLCV. Not an official NSE or BSE export, so treat levels as indicative. Authoritative fallback is the NSE daily archive https://archives.nseindia.com/content/indices/ind_close_all_DDMMYYYY.csv which only reaches back to about 2018-09 and needs one request per day.

toi.name: Times of India News Headlines
toi.citation: Kulkarni, Rohit (2020). Times of India News Headlines. Harvard Dataverse. https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/DPQMQH
toi.provenance: Harvard Dataverse DOI 10.7910/DVN/DPQMQH, the official publisher of the dataset. Single outlet (TOI), English only, headlines only, no article body.

rq1_topic_mix.artefact_note: A single raw category holding this share of a year indicates a change in how the publisher filed content, not a change in reader interest. Affected years need this caveat in the report.

fact.value: See largest_moves for the ranked table.
fact.caution: Shares are within-year, so the partial year does not distort them. Raw counts across years are not comparable.

rq2_bursts.finding: No month is a volume outlier. Within-year volume CV is at most 0.035, and the busiest month of each year runs only 2-5% above its own mean. The archive's headline volume behaves like a fixed editorial capacity rather than a response to news intensity.
rq2_bursts.counter_signal_summary: The single largest departure is `negative_rate` in 2020-04 at z = -2.63. In 5 of the 10 event months (2019-02, 2019-05, 2020-03, 2020-04, 2020-05) every one of the desks predicted to rise — Health, Sports, Entertainment — fell below its norm instead. That is a specific prediction failing, not a vague absence of signal. For scale, 81 of 154 measures sit below −0.5 SD, against roughly 47.5 expected by chance. That count is **not** offered as a significance test: the measures share months and are correlated, so their z-scores are not independent and the count is only shown so it is not hidden.
rq2_bursts.counter_signal_note: Derived from the measured z-scores above, not asserted. Note that these are departures from the norm, not dramatic swings: the largest is around 1.5 standard deviations on a series this flat.

fact.caution: This is a NULL result and it is the answer. Monthly volume is flat within each year, so no month is a statistical outlier. Lowering the threshold until a spike appeared would be choosing a threshold to manufacture a finding.

excluded_uninformative.reason: These carry no editorial subject, so their score measures the absence of a filing decision rather than the language used. They are excluded from the headline ranking.

sensitivity.stability_note: `Unknown` appears as the top topic at some thresholds because it is a filing gap, not a subject. Stability is judged on the informative topics only; the raw count is reported alongside so the difference is visible rather than hidden.
sensitivity.note: A ranking that changes its top topic as the cut-off moves is an artefact of the cut-off. Both facts are reported.

fact.unit: risk-signal rate, share of headlines over the sensationalism threshold
fact.caution: A STYLE measure on unlabelled headlines. It is a risk-signal rate and is NOT a fake-news rate. The threshold is the measured 95th percentile, a chosen cut-off, so the report must show the sensitivity table.

rq4_clusters.concentration_note: One cluster holds 94.88% of the sample and 3 further clusters hold at least 1% each. A high silhouette in this shape does not mean the corpus is well clustered: it means a small, well-separated topical minority exists and the remainder is undifferentiated. Read the score and the shape together.
rq4_clusters.k_note: Silhouette peaks at k=4 and falls away on both sides, so this k is a genuine optimum rather than an edge of the search range.

stability.note: The same documents are clustered twice with different K-Means seeds, so only the initialisation varies. High agreement means the partition is a property of the data; low agreement means the clusters are an artefact of the starting points.

fact.unit: silhouette score, higher is better separated
fact.caution: Read this with the cluster sizes, not alone. Silhouette rewards a large cluster sitting far from a few small tight ones, and that is the shape here: most headlines are undifferentiated while a small topical minority is cleanly separated. The score also depends entirely on the TF-IDF settings — an earlier run that admitted numerals and stop words measured 0.068 on the same data.

rq5_association_rules.redundancy_note: 313 of 644 rules are tautologies with lift exactly 1.000: the consequent is implied by the antecedent, as in `2015 => Local`. The transaction items are not independent — the sensational flag and the sentiment band are derived from the same score, and a year implies every other item carrying that year. Redundant items inflate the rule count without adding information, which is why 331 substantive rules are reported alongside the 644 total.
rq5_association_rules.lift_caveat: The highest-lift table is not dominated by the partial final period. Lift is still maximised by rare consequents in general, so the confidence table below is the more informative of the two.

keyword_run.caveat: Mean 1.992 items per transaction. The 300-term vocabulary is dominated by functional words, so these transactions are close to empty and the rules are weak by construction. Reported for completeness, not as a finding.

fact.caution: Association, not causation. A rule states two attributes co-occur more often than chance. Transactions are ATTRIBUTES, not keywords: the 300-term keyword vocabulary yields only 1.992 items per headline and produced zero rules at these thresholds, so keyword rules would have reported sparsity as a pattern.

significance_accounting.note: A significant result among many tests is expected. Count the significant results against the expected false positives before treating any of them as a finding.

volatility.note: Volatility is null until 20 sessions are available, so this uses 1235 of the trading days in the window. Association only. A significant coefficient here is not evidence of an effect: headline volume and market volatility both respond to the same underlying events, and nothing here separates their directions.

fact.unit: largest absolute Pearson r against daily RETURN, across measures and lags
fact.caution: ASSOCIATION ONLY. Against daily returns the relationship is negligible. Against 20-day VOLATILITY it is not: log headline volume correlates at about -0.28, which is a real association and still not an effect, because both respond to the same underlying events.

confusion_matrix.reading: row = actual class, column = predicted. The bottom-left cell is fake statements missed, which is the expensive error.

rq7_classifier.upper_bound_caveat: Part of IFND's Fake class is LSTM-generated augmentation of real statements, which is easier to distinguish than a fake article written by a person. This accuracy is therefore an upper bound on performance against genuine misinformation.

fact.unit: accuracy on a held-out 30% test split
fact.caution: The ONLY accuracy claim in this project, because IFND is the only source with ground truth. The majority baseline is 0.659049, not 0.5, so accuracy alone is meaningless. Part of the Fake class is LSTM-augmented, so this is an UPPER BOUND.

checks.detail: 1,113,427 rows, floor for a rate is 1000

outcomes.headline: Three of seven questions produced no result, or a result that reads better than it is. Those are reported with the measurement that establishes them.

outcomes.question: Do national events show up as spikes in news volume?
outcomes.headline: No. Headline volume carries no news signal.
outcomes.detail: Within-year volume varies by at most 0.0352, and 0 months out of 6 clear a z-score of 2. March 2020, the month of the national lockdown, sits 2.5% above its own year mean.
outcomes.evidence: In 5 of 10 listed event months, all three desks predicted to rise — Health, Sports and Entertainment — fell instead.
outcomes.caution: This data cannot distinguish a genuinely quota-driven newsroom from a sampling artefact of the publisher's export. Both produce the same signature.

outcomes.question: Do the headlines cluster into topics on their own?
outcomes.headline: Partly. Structure exists, but it covers a small minority.
outcomes.detail: Silhouette 0.2582, which clears the conventional 0.25 threshold — but one cluster holds 94.88% of the corpus. The small clusters find money terms (`rs crore`, `lakh`), traffic and crime (`road`, `accident`, `killed`) and age copy (`old`, `year old`).
outcomes.evidence: None of those is a topic in the publisher's own taxonomy, so the clustering found writing patterns rather than desks. An earlier run measured 0.068 and was wrong: the feature pipeline was admitting numerals and stop words.
outcomes.caution: Silhouette rewards one large cluster sitting far from a few small tight ones, so the score and the shape must be read together.

outcomes.question: Do headlines relate to the market?
outcomes.headline: Not to daily returns. Yes, to volatility — and the direction is unexplained.
outcomes.detail: Against returns the strongest correlation is 0.0748, and the one significant lag out of the fifteen tested is what chance produces. Against 20-day volatility, log business-headline volume correlates at -0.28272 (p < 0.0001, 7.993% of variance): busier headline days go with calmer markets.
outcomes.evidence: Fifteen lag tests at alpha 0.05 produce about 0.75 false positives, so a single p below 0.05 is the expected outcome of running the tests, not a discovery.
outcomes.caution: Association only. Headline volume and volatility both respond to the same underlying events, and nothing here identifies a direction of effect.

outcomes.question: Which topics use the most sensational language?
outcomes.headline: `Education` stands out, at 10.94% against a 3.77% corpus rate.
outcomes.evidence: `Unknown` tops the raw ranking at 17.29% and is excluded: it is a filing gap rather than a subject, so its score measures the absence of a filing decision.
outcomes.caution: A style measure on unlabelled headlines. It is a risk-signal rate and never a fake-news rate. The threshold is the measured 95th percentile, a chosen cut-off.

outcomes.question: Which co-occurrence patterns exist?
outcomes.headline: 644 rules, found identically by two independent algorithms.
outcomes.detail: FP-Growth is 0.65x faster on identical input, and 313 of the rules are tautologies counted separately.
outcomes.evidence: Apriori and FP-Growth return the same rule set, which is asserted: they search the same itemsets, so a difference would mean one is broken. The keyword vocabulary produced zero rules and is reported as a finding about the feature.
outcomes.caution: Association, not causation. A rule states two attributes co-occur more often than chance.

outcomes.question: Can a classifier separate real statements from fake ones?
outcomes.headline: 95.71% against a 65.90% majority baseline.
outcomes.evidence: The model was chosen on training cross-validated accuracy and the test split was scored once. Accuracy alone would flatter a model that learned nothing, because always answering 'real' already scores the baseline.
outcomes.caution: An upper bound. Part of IFND's Fake class is LSTM-generated augmentation, which is far easier to distinguish than a fake written by a person.

outcomes.question: How did the topic mix change across the window?
outcomes.headline: `Local` is 69.95% of the window, and one filing artefact dominates the story.
outcomes.detail: `business.international-business` is 11.1% of all 2017 headlines and 0.2% of 2018. A naive topic-mix analysis would report that as a change in what India was reading.
outcomes.evidence: 1 raw category holds an implausible share of a single year, which means the publisher changed how it filed content.
outcomes.caution: 2015 is a partial year, so every trend statement is a within-year share and raw counts across years are never compared.

honesty_rules: On the unlabelled TOI corpus every style measure is a RISK-SIGNAL rate. It is never a fake-news rate.
Only the IFND classifier states an accuracy, because IFND is the only source with ground truth.
Correlations are associations. No result in this project identifies an effect of news on markets.
Association rules state co-occurrence, never causation.
2015 is a partial year and is excluded from year-on-year comparison.
A negative result is reported as a negative result, with the measurement that establishes it.
